paragraphs: A contextual bandit chooses an action using information about the current situation and learns from the rewards it observes. This paper studies how an attacker can manipulate that learning process. The attacker’s objective is to steer choices toward a preferred action, potentially benefiting a seller or publisher at someone else’s expense.

The authors examine attacks that alter rewards or contexts. In the scenarios analyzed, an attacker can make a linear contextual bandit select any desired action on T − o(T) of T rounds. This means the fraction of rounds following the attacker’s preference approaches one as the horizon grows. Meanwhile, the cumulative modification cost grows only as O(log T).

The paper also considers targeting a single context, such as one user. It gives sufficient conditions for such an attack to be feasible and an efficient attack algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the proposed approaches. Together, the results show how relatively modest manipulation can have a persistent effect on the studied learning systems.
neurips-2020-adversarial-attacks-on-line.tldr: Under the studied attack scenarios, logarithmic-cost manipulation can steer linear contextual bandits toward an attacker’s preferred action on nearly every round.

paragraphs: CoinPress addresses a basic statistical task under privacy constraints: estimating the mean and covariance of data with multiple variables. The mean summarizes typical values, while covariance describes how variables vary together. The paper develops simple estimators that satisfy differential privacy and remain accurate with small sample sizes for multivariate sub-Gaussian data.

The motivation is a gap between theoretical accuracy and practical usefulness. According to the authors, earlier estimators can struggle with small datasets or multiple variables, or require users to supply strong prior estimates of the parameters. Those requirements matter because estimating the parameters is precisely the task the user wants to perform.

The authors support their methods with both mathematical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real datasets. Their asymptotic error rates match leading theoretical bounds, while the reported empirical comparisons outperform previous methods. These findings connect two different goals: maintaining favorable error behavior as sample size grows and delivering useful accuracy when data are limited. The stated distributional setting is central to those results.
neurips-2020-coinpress-practical-private.tldr: CoinPress provides differentially private mean and covariance estimators with strong theoretical rates and improved empirical accuracy at small sample sizes.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning works backward from demonstrated behavior to a reward that can explain it. Common maximum-entropy approaches repeatedly estimate values while updating that reward, which can slow learning. This paper introduces algorithms that need to solve the decision process underlying the demonstrations only once to recover the expert policy.

The approach places a probabilistic assumption about demonstrated behavior inside a Q-learning formulation. Inverse Action-value Iteration analytically recovers an underlying reward in closed form. Related sampling-based versions avoid requiring an environment model. Function approximation extends the approach to continuous states, while an optional constrained version seeks a policy close to the demonstrator’s behavior that also satisfies predefined hard constraints.

On Objectworld, the authors report speedups reaching several orders of magnitude over the compared maximum-entropy methods. They also apply Deep Constrained Inverse Q-learning to autonomous lane changes in the SUMO simulator. Training on demonstrations corresponding to 30 minutes produces competent driving in that setting. These results illustrate both the computational benefit and the possibility of incorporating explicit behavioral requirements.
neurips-2020-deep-inverse-q-learning-wit.tldr: A Q-learning formulation recovers rewards from demonstrations more efficiently and can learn imitation policies subject to predefined hard constraints.

paragraphs: Local feature methods identify image locations and describe them so corresponding points can be matched across images. Learning this whole process together is difficult because selecting a sparse set of keypoints and deciding matches involve discrete choices. DISK addresses that obstacle by using principles from reinforcement learning to train the feature system end to end.

Its training objective directly favors producing many correct feature matches. A probabilistic model represents the relevant choices, allowing the method to learn despite their discreteness. The authors emphasize that this model keeps training behavior close to inference behavior while retaining convergence properties sufficient for reliable training from scratch.

The learned features can also be extracted densely while remaining discriminative, meaning that many extracted features can still be distinguished from one another. This finding challenges assumptions about which image locations make useful keypoints. The authors report state-of-the-art results on three public benchmarks. The contribution therefore combines a way to optimize the complete matching pipeline with empirical evidence that dense feature extraction can work well.
neurips-2020-disk-learning-local-feature.tldr: DISK uses reinforcement-learning principles to train discrete keypoint selection and matching end to end, producing dense, discriminative local features.

paragraphs: Many geometric learning computations use matrices whose entries are determined by a formula and input data, such as distances between points or kernel values. This paper builds a toolbox around that symbolic representation. It extends standard machine learning frameworks with support for these computations on both CPUs and GPUs, emphasizing fast execution and low memory use.

The interface turns generic Python code into compiled binaries while retaining flexibility across geometric operations. The authors report performance competitive with specialized geometric libraries, including FAISS for nearest-neighbor search. The significance is that a common programming abstraction can support varied computations without giving up the speed associated with tools built for particular tasks.

The evaluation covers Gaussian modeling, nearest-neighbor search, geometric deep learning, non-Euclidean embeddings, and optimal transport. For the tested geometric problems involving one thousand to one million samples and dimensions from one to one hundred, speedups over baseline GPU implementations reach two orders of magnitude. That is a reported maximum within the evaluated range, rather than a uniform improvement for every workload.
neurips-2020-fast-geometric-learning-wit.tldr: A symbolic-matrix toolbox makes varied geometric computations fast and memory-efficient, with reported GPU speedups reaching two orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Matching locations between two images becomes difficult when several regions look alike. A conventional feature correlation layer compares pairs of feature vectors through scalar products, producing a volume of possible correspondences. The paper argues that these isolated comparisons are insufficient to resolve competing matches among similar regions, which can harm the larger vision task.

GOCor replaces that layer with a fully differentiable matching module. Its correspondence volume comes from an internal optimization procedure that explicitly accounts for similar regions in the scene. It can also learn spatial matching priors, using regularities in how locations correspond to help resolve further ambiguities. Differentiability lets the module participate in the surrounding network’s training.

The authors analyze GOCor through extensive ablation experiments and integrate it into state-of-the-art networks. They report significant improvements over the feature correlation layer for geometric matching, optical flow, and dense semantic matching. These findings support treating correspondence estimation as an optimization problem within the network, giving the matching stage more capacity to address ambiguity than individual feature comparisons provide.
neurips-2020-gocor-bringing-globally-opt.tldr: GOCor replaces pairwise feature correlation with a differentiable optimization module that resolves matching ambiguities and improves several dense correspondence tasks.

paragraphs: Generating a textured 3D person from one image requires handling both visible appearance and body regions hidden from view. This paper proposes a texture transfer model that uses semantic human parsing: a representation identifying the person’s body parts. That input supplies shape and pose information while preserving where the semantic parts lie.

The model learns to improve predictions for unseen regions through consistency across views of the same person. During training, textures predicted from two views are exchanged and used to render images. This makes the relationship between views part of the learning signal. Perceptual loss and total variation regularization guide the rendered images toward the inputs without requiring additional 3D texture supervision.

Experiments use pedestrian images and fashion photographs. The authors report higher-quality textures with convincing details compared with other texture generation methods. The approach matters because it combines a structured description of the body with a training signal that connects viewpoints. Although prediction uses one image, training across views helps address appearance that the single input cannot directly show.
neurips-2020-human-parsing-based-texture.tldr: Body-part parsing and cross-view training help generate detailed 3D human textures from one image without additional 3D texture supervision.

paragraphs: Kernel methods offer a principled approach to nonparametric learning, but straightforward implementations become expensive as datasets grow. This paper tackles that computational barrier by developing a solver designed to use GPU hardware efficiently. Its focus is on making the numerical work behind kernel learning practical at very large scales.

The solver combines preconditioned gradient optimization with GPU acceleration and parallel execution across multiple GPUs. It also implements out-of-core versions of common linear algebra operations, allowing those operations to work with data beyond what fits in the relevant fast memory. Further improvements adjust numerical precision across operations and make matrix-vector multiplication more efficient.

These choices address several sources of computational cost together: the optimization procedure, data handling, arithmetic, and hardware utilization. The authors report dramatic experimental speedups on datasets containing billions of points while maintaining state-of-the-art performance. They also provide an accessible software library. The findings show that careful numerical and implementation design can substantially expand the scale at which kernel methods are useful.
neurips-2020-kernel-methods-through-the-.tldr: A GPU-focused kernel solver combines numerical and hardware optimizations to achieve dramatic reported speedups on datasets with billions of points.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when each point belongs to one or more protected groups and each cluster must satisfy representation constraints. The goal is to form k clusters under the k-center objective while avoiding excessive or insufficient representation of groups. Fairness is therefore part of the clustering problem, alongside the usual concern for clustering quality.

The authors develop a randomized algorithm with a 3-approximation guarantee for the k-center objective, improving the previous factor of 4. An approximation factor describes how the algorithm’s objective value compares with an optimal solution under the stated problem formulation. Reducing that factor strengthens the theoretical quality guarantee for a problem that also imposes group representation requirements.

Experiments on real datasets assess both efficiency and the resulting clusters. The authors report improvements in runtime and clustering cost over the existing state of the art, with similar fairness violations. This distinction matters: the empirical gains concern speed and clustering quality while preserving comparable fairness behavior. The paper combines a tighter approximation result with evidence of practical scalability.
neurips-2020-kfc-a-scalable-approximatio.tldr: KFC improves fair k-center clustering’s approximation factor from 4 to 3 and reports faster, lower-cost clustering with comparable fairness violations.

paragraphs: Facial expressions and facial action units describe behavior at different levels, but they are related through anatomy and the combinations that form coherent expressions. This paper uses those dependencies to connect expression recognition with action-unit detection. The central idea is to make general knowledge about their relationship useful during neural-network training.

A constrained optimization method first encodes probabilistic expression–action-unit dependencies in a Bayesian network. That network supplies weak supervision for the action-unit detector. A separate facial expression model is learned from data, after which the two models are trained jointly to refine their learning. This gives the detector guidance from structured knowledge while also allowing the models to learn from observations.

Benchmark evaluations show improvements for both expression recognition and action-unit detection. The authors also report competitive action-unit detection without action-unit annotations, and good generalization of the knowledge-based Bayesian network across datasets. These findings suggest that explicitly modeling relationships between labels can reduce reliance on direct annotations while helping both related recognition tasks.
neurips-2020-knowledge-augmented-deep-ne.tldr: A Bayesian network of expression–action-unit relationships guides joint neural learning, improving both tasks and enabling competitive action-unit detection without its annotations.

paragraphs: RichLQR describes a control problem with a simple hidden structure and complicated observations. The underlying state is low-dimensional, evolves linearly, and incurs quadratic costs. The agent, however, receives high-dimensional nonlinear observations, such as camera images. Learning must therefore connect those observations to the hidden state needed for effective control.

The paper assumes access to a decoder function class flexible enough to represent the mapping from observations to latent states. Under this setup, the proposed RichID algorithm learns a near-optimal policy with sample complexity scaling only with latent-state dimension and decoder-class capacity. This ties the data requirement to the hidden control structure and the difficulty of decoding it.

RichID accesses the decoder class through a least-squares regression oracle and is oracle-efficient. Its computational statement is therefore expressed in terms of access to that regression capability. The authors describe the result as, to their knowledge, the first provable sample-complexity guarantee for continuous control with an unknown nonlinearity in the system model. The decoder assumption is central to making that guarantee possible.
neurips-2020-learning-the-linear-quadrat.tldr: RichID provably learns near-optimal control from nonlinear observations when a sufficiently expressive decoder class can recover the low-dimensional latent state.

paragraphs: Online decisions can incur both an immediate cost and a cost for changing the previous decision. Those switching costs connect choices across time, making forecasts useful. Yet looking farther ahead can also expose the decision maker to less accurate predictions. This paper studies how to use forecasts while controlling the harm from their errors.

The proposed Receding Horizon Inexact Gradient algorithm, RHIG, uses predictions no more than W steps ahead. The authors analyze dynamic regret in terms of both environmental change and prediction error. Their bounds suggest choosing the forecast horizon by balancing these factors: a longer view can help anticipate changes, but unreliable distant forecasts can undermine that benefit.

The analysis also covers a stochastic prediction-error model with correlated errors, providing expected-regret and concentration bounds. Correlation matters because forecast mistakes need not occur independently across time. Numerical tests apply RHIG to quadrotor tracking. The paper’s contribution is a gradient-based decision rule together with theoretical guidance for selecting how far into an uncertain future to plan.
neurips-2020-leveraging-predictions-in-s.tldr: RHIG limits its forecast horizon and uses regret analysis to balance changing environments against increasingly unreliable long-term predictions.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn control behavior but can require substantial exploration before producing a strong policy. When an agent encounters a sequence of tasks, starting each learning process without using earlier knowledge wastes an opportunity. This paper develops a lifelong learning method that brings accumulated knowledge into policy-gradient training for new tasks.

The method trains lifelong function approximators directly through policy gradients. Its key feature is that previous knowledge can influence the entire training process, allowing transfer to contribute while the new policy is still being learned. The factored-policy approach is intended to support both efficient acquisition of new behavior and retention of behavior learned earlier.

Across the challenging domains evaluated, the authors report faster learning and convergence to better policies than both single-task and lifelong learning baselines. They also report completely avoiding catastrophic forgetting in those experiments. These are empirical findings within the evaluated domains. Together, they support the possibility of using shared experience to improve new-task learning without sacrificing previously acquired control skills.
neurips-2020-lifelong-policy-gradient-le.tldr: A lifelong policy-gradient method uses accumulated knowledge throughout training, improving learning speed and policy quality without forgetting in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial data augmentation trains a model using deliberately challenging variations of its training data. The difficulty is deciding how to generate useful variations that differ substantially from the source distribution. This paper introduces a regularization term that gives this process a principled objective instead of relying entirely on manually chosen perturbation heuristics.

The authors derive the regularizer from the information bottleneck principle, obtaining a maximum-entropy formulation. Its intuitive effect is to encourage changes to the source distribution that increase the current model’s predictive uncertainty. Those uncertain examples provide challenging training inputs, with the aim of improving robustness to unforeseen distribution shifts or corruptions.

Experiments on three standard benchmarks show statistically significant improvements over the existing state of the art. The findings support uncertainty as a useful signal for constructing adversarial training distributions in the evaluated settings. The contribution links a theoretical derivation to a practical augmentation mechanism: make the current model less certain when generating examples, then use those examples to strengthen its training.
neurips-2020-maximum-entropy-adversarial.tldr: A maximum-entropy regularizer generates adversarial training examples that increase predictive uncertainty, improving robustness and generalization on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Class imbalance makes learning difficult when some classes appear much more often than others. Resampling and reweighting methods often depend on heuristics whose assumptions may fail on complex tasks. MESA addresses this by learning how to sample training data, with the sampling strategy directed toward improving the final evaluation metric.

The framework repeatedly resamples the training set to train multiple classifiers, which form a cascade ensemble. A meta-sampler controls the adaptive sampling strategy. Its training is separated from classifier training: the meta-sampler learns independently from task-agnostic metadata. This separation is designed to make the sampler broadly compatible with existing learning models and efficient to apply to new tasks.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, robustness, and transferability. The significance lies in treating sampling as a learned component that can move between tasks, while the classifiers remain separate learning components. The reported results support this approach as a way to handle imbalance without committing every application to a fixed sampling heuristic.
neurips-2020-mesa-boost-ensemble-imbalan.tldr: MESA learns a transferable sampling strategy for imbalanced data and uses it to train an adaptive cascade of classifiers.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks while retaining useful knowledge from earlier ones. MERLIN approaches this problem through an assumption about neural-network weights: weights that solve a task come from a shared meta-distribution. Learning that distribution provides a way to represent knowledge accumulated across tasks.

The method learns and consolidates the meta-distribution incrementally as new information arrives. The study uses an online continual learning setting in which the model sees each data point only once. That restriction makes the ability to preserve accumulated information especially relevant, because the model cannot simply count on repeated access to the same observations.

Experiments use continual learning benchmarks based on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-ImageNet. The authors report consistent improvement over five baselines, including a recent state-of-the-art method. These results support the promise of consolidating a distribution over task-solving weights in the tested online setting. They provide empirical evidence for the approach’s usefulness in balancing ongoing adaptation with retention of earlier knowledge.
neurips-2020-meta-consolidation-for-cont.tldr: MERLIN incrementally consolidates a shared distribution over task-solving network weights, improving online continual learning across four benchmark families.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a framework for problems including much of the optimization involved in training generative adversarial networks. Existing convergence analyses often assume monotonicity, a structural property that these problems may lack. This paper proposes optimistic dual extrapolation, OptDE, to obtain guarantees under specified coherent non-monotone conditions.

OptDE uses one gradient evaluation per iteration. When a weak solution exists, the authors prove convergence to a strong solution with O(1/epsilon²) complexity, matching the best existing rate for methods using two gradient evaluations. Under the stronger condition that a sigma-weak solution exists, the guarantee improves to O(log(1/epsilon)). These improvements depend on the stated solution assumptions.

For monotone problems, the paper also establishes a near-optimal O((1/epsilon) log(1/epsilon)) guarantee measured by a restricted strong merit function. It extends the analysis to stochastic settings and derives corresponding convergence results. The contribution combines lower gradient-evaluation demands per iteration with guarantees spanning several problem structures; it does not make the non-monotone assumptions unnecessary.
neurips-2020-optimistic-dual-extrapolati.tldr: OptDE uses one gradient evaluation per iteration while achieving strong convergence guarantees under specified coherent non-monotone and monotone conditions.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks must change to learn new tasks, but those changes can disrupt dynamics that support earlier behavior. This paper introduces a learning rule that organizes new learning around the computations already established in the network. Its goal is to preserve old abilities while leaving room for new ones.

The rule protects network dynamics within activity-defined subspaces used by previous tasks. New dynamics that would interfere are encouraged to develop in orthogonal subspaces. At the same time, the method permits reuse of previously learned dynamical motifs where possible. It therefore combines separation of conflicting computations with sharing when existing dynamics can support another task.

On a set of neuroscience tasks, the authors report eliminating catastrophic interference and substantially improving on previous continual learning algorithms. Dynamical systems analysis shows that similar tasks can reuse similar structures, enabling faster sequential learning. The paper also identifies differences in organization between sequential and simultaneous training. These findings connect retention and transfer to how task computations occupy the network’s activity space.
neurips-2020-organizing-recurrent-networ.tldr: A recurrent-network learning rule protects prior dynamics, separates interfering computations, and reuses compatible structures to support continual learning.

paragraphs: Sequential planning usually evaluates a sequence of decisions by adding its rewards. Some applications require a different criterion: safe control, for example, may prioritize the lowest reward encountered. This paper studies planning with a general function of the rewards across the horizon, allowing objectives that a simple sum cannot express.

The authors develop an algorithm for deterministic systems using techniques from sketching algorithms. They show that efficient planning is possible for a large class of objective functions when the function is unchanged by permuting its reward inputs and meets additional technical conditions. Permutation symmetry means that the objective depends on the collection of rewards rather than their order.

The paper also establishes worst-case intractability when any of its conditions is removed. This gives the conditions a role beyond making the proposed analysis convenient: dropping them permits hard problems in the broader class. The result identifies a tractable region for planning beyond cumulative reward while clarifying why unrestricted general objectives can be computationally difficult.
neurips-2020-planning-with-general-objec.tldr: A sketching-based algorithm enables deterministic planning for general reward objectives under conditions whose removal permits worst-case intractability.

paragraphs: Sequences of neural spikes are hypothesized to support functions such as working memory, movement, and learning. Discovering those sequences without labels is difficult. This paper develops a point process model that describes sequences at the level of individual spikes and represents their occurrences as a small number of marked events in continuous time.

The model addresses three shortcomings of a preceding convolutive nonnegative matrix factorization approach: discretizing spike times, using a suboptimal least-squares criterion, and lacking uncertainty estimates for predictions or parameters. The continuous-time event representation makes sequence occurrences especially sparse while allowing fine timing information to remain part of the modeling problem.

The authors also introduce learnable time-warping parameters so a sequence can occur over different durations. This accommodates duration variability that has been observed experimentally in neural circuits. Demonstrations on songbird higher vocal center and rodent hippocampus recordings illustrate the model’s advantages. The contribution links precise event timing, uncertainty estimation, and flexible sequence duration within one framework for unsupervised discovery.
neurips-2020-point-process-models-for-se.tldr: A continuous-time point process model detects neural spike sequences while representing uncertainty and accommodating sequences with varying durations.

paragraphs: Prediction with expert advice asks a learner to make decisions using several competing advisers and their observed losses. This paper considers a mixed setting: the underlying environment generates losses stochastically, but an adversary can moderately corrupt the feedback the learner receives. The challenge is to retain the benefits of a benign environment despite manipulated observations.

The authors analyze a variant of Multiplicative Weights whose step sizes decrease over time. They prove constant regret in this setting and optimal performance across a wide range of environments, regardless of the injected corruption’s magnitude. Constant regret concerns how regret grows with the time horizon; the statement should not be read as saying corruption has no effect on performance.

The results also distinguish two frameworks often viewed as comparable: Follow the Regularized Leader and Online Mirror Descent. For experts under corrupted stochastic feedback, the authors show strictly inferior regret performance for Online Mirror Descent. The finding makes the choice of update framework consequential even when the underlying, uncorrupted losses are stochastic.
neurips-2020-prediction-with-corrupted-e.tldr: Decreasing-step Multiplicative Weights achieves constant regret under corrupted stochastic feedback, while the analysis separates FTRL from the worse-performing OMD framework.

paragraphs: Normalization changes neural-network training in ways that conventional optimization intuitions may not capture. This paper begins a mathematical framework for studying those differences by modeling stochastic gradient descent trajectories with a stochastic differential equation. The equation includes a noise term representing randomness in the gradients.

The analysis introduces an intrinsic learning rate equal to the ordinary learning rate multiplied by the weight-decay factor. This parameter governs how the effective speed of learning changes and reaches equilibrium in the model. The authors also use theory and experiments to challenge the belief that good generalization requires a large learning rate at the start of training.

Further experiments, supported by mathematical intuition, suggest that the number of steps needed to reach equilibrium in function space scales inversely with the intrinsic learning rate. This is faster than the exponential-time convergence bound implied by the SDE analysis. The authors call this the Fast Equilibrium Conjecture and suggest it may explain Batch Normalization’s effectiveness. That scaling remains a conjecture, distinct from the formal analysis.
neurips-2020-reconciling-modern-deep-lea.tldr: An SDE framework identifies learning rate times weight decay as an intrinsic training parameter and motivates a conjecture about fast equilibrium in normalized networks.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks use graph structure to learn features, often encouraging neighboring nodes to have similar activations. Too much similarity can make different nodes difficult to distinguish, a problem called oversmoothing. This paper augments conventional graph convolution with geometric scattering transforms and residual convolutions to preserve more informative variation.

The scattering component provides band-pass filtering of graph signals, giving the model access to information that ordinary smoothing can suppress. Residual convolutions then help remove high-frequency noise from the resulting features. The two additions serve related but distinct purposes: retaining useful differences among nodes and cleaning up unwanted variation.

The authors provide theoretical results establishing complementary benefits of scattering and conventional GCN features. Experiments on semi-supervised node classification show advantages over leading graph neural networks, including a graph attention network that also addresses oversmoothing. The findings support combining different ways of processing graph signals so that structural regularity can aid classification without erasing distinctions that matter for identifying nodes.
neurips-2020-scattering-gcn-overcoming-o.tldr: Scattering GCN combines band-pass graph features with residual convolutions to reduce oversmoothing and improve semi-supervised node classification.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can quantify uncertainty, but computing it can be expensive in models with many parameters. Variational Bayes offers a scalable approximation. This paper studies a mean-field spike-and-slab approximation for sparse high-dimensional logistic regression, using priors designed for selecting which variables belong in the model.

The authors establish finite-sample theoretical guarantees when the underlying truth is sparse. They measure accuracy both through parameter error in the l2 sense and through prediction loss, obtaining optimal minimax convergence rates. These guarantees show that the approximation can achieve the best worst-case rate in the studied sparse setting, rather than sacrificing that rate simply to gain computational scalability.

The algorithm does not need knowledge of the unknown truth to attain its optimality result. The authors use this to illuminate effective prior choices. A numerical study also reports improved performance over common sparse variational Bayes approaches. The paper thus combines theoretical support for a particular approximation with empirical evidence that its prior structure can improve practical inference.
neurips-2020-spike-and-slab-variational-.tldr: Spike-and-slab variational Bayes achieves optimal theoretical rates for sparse logistic regression and improves on common sparse VB approaches in a numerical study.

paragraphs: When an environment changes, a useful model must adapt without needlessly discarding what it already knows. This paper proposes transferring a high-dimensional model from a source domain to a target domain through two l1 penalties. One encourages sparse parameter estimates, while the other encourages sparse differences between source and target parameters.

The second penalty makes adaptation selective: the method favors changing only some parameters while retaining others. The authors establish a tight estimation-error bound in a stationary environment and show that the target estimate stays identical to the source estimate when residuals are small. This gives a precise condition under which the method preserves existing knowledge.

The analysis also establishes consistency with the underlying function even when environmental change has made the source estimate mistaken. Thus, the method can retain a suitable source model while still correcting an unsuitable one under the analyzed conditions. Empirical results support its ability to balance stability and plasticity, connecting those theoretical properties to the practical problem of deciding how much to change.
neurips-2020-transfer-learning-via-ell-1.tldr: Penalizing both model parameters and changes from a source model enables sparse adaptation while balancing retention and correction.
